title: How rod cells give us night vision
examples: How do we see in the dark?
Why does it take a while for my eyes to adjust to the dark?

explain.say: Your retina has two kinds of light-sensing cell. Cones handle bright light and colour, while rods are so sensitive that they keep working in moonlight and starlight.

explain.say: Rods are the night-time cells. There are about 120 million of them in each eye, and they can respond to tiny amounts of light, but they all report the same way, so they cannot tell colours apart.

explain.say: Cones crowd into the very centre of the retina, where you look straight at things. That is why in dim light the centre of your vision is weakest and colours fade away.

draw.verdict: At night the rods take over, so the world turns grey

explain.say: Rods use a pigment called rhodopsin that bright light bleaches. In the dark it slowly rebuilds, so your night vision keeps getting better for about 20 to 30 minutes.

faq.a: Rod cells are light-sensing cells in the retina that are extremely sensitive to dim light. They let us see shapes and movement at night, but only in shades of grey.
asks: What do rods in the eye do?
How many rods are in the eye?

faq.q: Why does it take time for eyes to adjust to the dark?
faq.a: Bright light bleaches the pigment in rod cells, called rhodopsin. In the dark it is rebuilt slowly, so your eyes become more sensitive over about 20 to 30 minutes. A flash of bright light bleaches it again.
asks: Why can't I see when the lights go off?

faq.q: Why does everything look grey at night?
faq.a: In dim light only the rods are working. There is just one type of rod, so the brain has nothing to compare and cannot work out colours.
asks: Why can't we see colour in the dark?

faq.q: Why can you see a faint star better when you look slightly to the side?
faq.a: The centre of your retina is packed with cones and has almost no rods. Looking a little to one side puts the star's light on the rod-rich area around it, which is more sensitive in the dark.
asks: Why do faint stars disappear when I look straight at them?

faq.a: Cone cells are the retina's bright-light cells. They come in three types and give us colour and sharp detail, and they are packed most tightly in the centre of the retina.
asks: What is the difference between rods and cones?
Where are cones in the eye?

facts: Each human eye has roughly 120 million rods and 6 million cones.
Full dark adaptation of the rods takes about 20 to 30 minutes.
The pigment in rod cells is called rhodopsin, or visual purple, and it needs vitamin A to be made.
